To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the most commonly used screening tools are the FAMCARE, the Edmonton symptom assessment system, the palliative care screening tool, the palliative prognostic score, the support team assessment schedule and the palliative care outcome scale.
the majority of European palliative care providers use the EORTC QLQ-C15-PAL questionnaire for the identification of palliative care patients in primary care.

there is a need to improve identification of palliative care needs and that there are no validated tools available to identify patients who may benefit from palliative care interventions in primary care.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of patients with palliative needs and their subsequent management in the primary care setting, in particular, the role of the GP and the multidisciplinary team in the primary care environment.
how to identify patients with advanced chronic disease who may benefit from palliative care interventions, including early palliative care.
identifying the most useful tools for identifying patients with palliative and end of life care needs in the primary care setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
early identification of people with palliative care need in primary care is a complex process and there is little evidence of effective screening tools.
palliative assessment and care should start as early as possible and should be available to all patients, regardless of diagnosis, age, or prognosis.
early palliative care should not be restricted to patients with malignant diseases, but should also be provided for those with non-malignancies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tools available to identify patients in need of palliative care are not yet sufficient for primary care.
we are not yet able to identify patients with non-cancer palliative care needs early and reliably.

palliative assessment and care is not only needed for patients with advanced malignant disease, but also for people with non-malleable conditions; the assessment should be comprehensive, and not just focused on physical problems; and that palliative care is not only for people with a life-limiting illness, but for all people with serious health problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the identification of people who would benefit from palliative care is a complex process that requires the use of a variety of tools and approaches.

the tools used to identify people who would benefit from palliative care are not well validated and there is a need to develop and validate tools that can help identify people with palliative care need in primary care, and that can be used by a wide variety of healthcare providers.
